chapters.title: Chapter 3: Reading Trade War Signals as an Investor

lessons.title: Hedging and Sector Rotation Strategies During Trade Tensions

children.text: You can now read the signals before they hit the price. This lesson is about what to actually do with that read: how to tilt a portfolio through sector rotation, when currency and options hedges genuinely make sense, and when the correct action is simply to do nothing.

body.title: What Tends to Hold Up vs. What Tends to Wobble First

columns.label: Defensives (Tend to Hold Up)
points: FMCG: domestic consumption, minimal direct tariff exposure
Pharma: often carved out of tariffs, as you saw in Chapter 2
IT with a diversified, non-US-concentrated client base

columns.label: Cyclicals (Tend to Wobble First)
points: Metals: exposed to both direct tariffs and trade-diverted import dumping
Auto and auto components: global supply chains, tariff-sensitive
Export-heavy textiles, gems and jewellery: directly named in tariff orders
IT with concentrated US manufacturing or retail clients

children.text: Rotation should be a gradual tilt in fresh allocation and rebalancing, not a binary switch out of an entire portfolio on one headline. And before rotating at all, apply the Chapter 2 test: is this move actually trade-war-driven, broad-based, and showing up in other emerging markets too, or is it a domestic-specific or single-stock story wearing a trade war label? Rotating a portfolio in response to noise is how you end up paying transaction costs and taxes for a move that reverses in a week.
Currency Hedging: When You Actually Need It

markDefs.definition: Exchange-traded contracts to buy or sell a currency pair at a set price on a future date. NSE's USD/INR futures trade in lots of $1,000 and are accessible through most brokers offering the currency derivatives segment.

children.text: Most retail equity investors do not need a direct currency hedge. If you hold Indian equities in rupees and plan to spend in rupees, rupee depreciation does not directly cost you anything, it affects specific companies' input costs and export revenues, which is already reflected in the sector rotation above. Direct hedging matters more if you have actual foreign currency exposure: importers and exporters managing a business, or investors holding foreign assets who want to lock in a conversion rate.
on the USD/INR pair are how that hedge typically gets built, but for a pure equity portfolio, sector allocation is usually doing the same job more cheaply than a derivatives position would.

A protective put, buying a Nifty put option against an existing equity portfolio, is the most direct way to hedge broad market risk during a period you expect real volatility, a tariff deadline, an escalation threat, a major trade announcement due. If the market falls, the put gains value and offsets some of the portfolio's loss. If the market does not fall, you lose the premium paid, the cost of the insurance.

body.caption: Illustrative long Nifty put used as a portfolio hedge. Strike and premium are illustrative only, adjust to current Nifty levels and actual option prices before using this as a real hedge.

body.text: A hedge is not free, and it is not meant to be. Options lose value over time even if the market does nothing (time decay), so buying puts every time a tariff headline appears will steadily erode returns if the volatility you're hedging against does not actually materialize. Size a hedge to a specific, time-bound risk, a known tariff deadline, for example, rather than running it as a permanent position.

children.text: Gold and Global Diversification as Structural Hedges

Gold has historically moved with low or negative correlation to equities during risk-off episodes, for the reason you saw in Chapter 2: trade war fear pushes investors toward safe havens. Sovereign Gold Bonds carry a 2.5% annual interest on top of gold's price movement, and capital gains are tax-exempt for individual investors who hold to maturity, a genuine structural advantage over physical gold or most gold ETFs. International or US-focused mutual funds and ETFs offer a different kind of hedge: exposure that does not move with India-specific trade shocks. Note that Indian AMCs have periodically had to pause fresh subscriptions into overseas fund categories due to industry-wide RBI investment limits, so check whether a specific international fund is actually open for lump-sum or SIP investment before relying on it.

body.title: Build the Response
body.scenario: You hold a diversified Nifty-tracking portfolio plus individual positions in a textile exporter and an FMCG company. The US has just announced a new round of tariffs specifically targeting textile exports, effective in three weeks, and India VIX has jumped 20% on the news, while other emerging markets are largely flat.
body.prompt: Walk through what you would actually do, if anything, across your three holdings.
body.modelAnswer: First, apply the domestic-vs-global test from Chapter 2: other emerging markets being flat while India VIX jumps suggests this is a fairly India- and sector-specific shock, not a broad global risk-off event, which argues against a blunt, whole-portfolio hedge. The textile exporter is a direct loser and worth reviewing specifically, check its US revenue concentration before deciding whether to trim, rather than assuming the sector headline applies equally to this one company. The FMCG holding is a defensive with minimal direct exposure and probably needs no action. A time-bound Nifty put sized to the three-week window until the tariff takes effect could make sense if you specifically want to protect against broader spillover risk in that window, but it is optional insurance, not a required response, given the shock looks contained rather than systemic so far.

body.title: A Practical Trade War Playbook
steps: Confirm the shock is trade-war-driven and broad enough to matter, using the Chapter 2 checklist, before making any change
Rotate gradually toward defensives only if the shock looks broad-based and sustained, not on a single headline
Review direct-exposure holdings individually rather than selling an entire sector on a label
Reserve index options hedging for specific, time-bound risk windows, not as a standing position
Treat gold and international diversification as structural, slow-moving hedges you set up in calmer periods, not something you can build overnight mid-selloff

body.text: The best hedge against a trade war is usually already built before the trade war starts, through sector diversification and a small structural allocation to gold, not a scramble to buy puts after the headline breaks.

points: Sector rotation toward defensives (FMCG, carved-out pharma, utilities) and away from cyclicals (metals, autos, export-heavy textiles) should be a gradual tilt, confirmed by the Chapter 2 test for a genuine trade-war-driven move.
Most equity-only investors do not need direct currency hedges; sector allocation already captures most of that risk, currency futures matter more for those with direct forex exposure.
A protective Nifty put is a legitimate, time-bound hedge against a specific known risk window, but it costs premium and erodes value if used as a permanent position.
Sovereign Gold Bonds (2.5% annual interest, tax-exempt gains at maturity) and international diversification are structural hedges best built in calm periods, not assembled mid-crisis.
The strongest response to most trade war headlines is reviewing specific direct-exposure holdings individually, not rotating or hedging the entire portfolio on a single announcement.
